differences.title: 1. DATA MODEL
differences.leftDesc: InfluxDB organizes data into measurements with tag sets that form an index-like keyspace. Each point is stored with a timestamp and fields, enabling efficient tag filtering and time-bounded queries via internal series mapping.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse uses explicit tables with typed columns, typically optimized for wide fact tables. Time is just another column, while partitioning and primary key ordering (e.g., by time/device) drive read skipping and fast scans over columns.

differences.title: 2. INGESTION & WRITE PATH
differences.leftDesc: InfluxDB’s write path batches incoming line protocol points into shards and maintains WAL-style durability. Series are appended then compacted according to retention/downsampling policies, smoothing bursts while controlling on-disk layout.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse ingests rows into in-memory/temporary buffers (depending on engine) and persists them into parts. Background merge tree processes compact parts asynchronously, improving compression and scan locality without blocking front-end reads.

differences.title: 3. QUERY LANGUAGE & PLANNING
differences.leftDesc: InfluxDB commonly uses InfluxQL or Flux. The engine leverages series/tag selection and time filters to reduce scanned series, then executes windowed aggregations per series, often pushing down filters early in the plan.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse is SQL-native (with dialect specifics) and uses cost-based/heuristic optimizations like predicate pushdown, projection pruning, and sampling. The planner chooses which partitions/parts to read and orders execution around column access patterns.

differences.title: 4. STORAGE LAYOUT
differences.leftDesc: InfluxDB uses storage engines that write time-value pairs into structures like TSM blocks, partitioned into shards. Compacting reorganizes blocks for sequential reads, while high-cardinality tag series map to separate logical streams.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse’s MergeTree family stores data in sorted “parts” with primary-key-based ordering. Reads skip irrelevant parts using partition keys and min/max indices; compression codecs and column encodings reduce IO for scans and aggregations.

differences.title: 5. AGGREGATIONS & WINDOWING
differences.leftDesc: InfluxDB performs many aggregations by operating within each series’ time-ordered points. Window functions and downsampling can be computed per series, then combined, which keeps semantics aligned with tag-keyed streams.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse accelerates aggregations via vectorized execution and efficient hash-table/group-by strategies. Window-like operations often map to specialized execution paths, benefiting from ordered data and skipping to limit the working set.

differences.title: 6. HIGH-CARDINALITY HANDLING
differences.leftDesc: InfluxDB’s tag-indexing model is fast when tags are curated, but excessive unique tag combinations increase series count and index overhead. Tuning typically involves reducing tag cardinality and using fields or regex transforms carefully.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse handles high cardinality largely through efficient column encodings and sorting keys, but group-bys on extremely high-cardinality dimensions still cost memory/CPU. Choosing appropriate partition/order keys and approximate/rollup strategies matters.

differences.title: 7. REAL-TIME EVENT LOG USE
differences.leftDesc: InfluxDB supports near-real-time rollups via continuous queries and tasks, writing aggregated results into separate measurements. This lets dashboards query precomputed windows while ingestion remains optimized for time-series appends.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse implements real-time derived data using materialized views over streaming inserts into Kafka/other integrations. Aggregations are computed as data arrives and stored in target tables, enabling low-latency reads with batch-like merge efficiency.
